procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 27, 1969, of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeals
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court affirmed the conviction of the appellants (Khandu Sonu Dhobi and Bhikanrao Rambhau Khaimar) under sections 218, 477A, and 409 of the Indian Penal Code, all read with section 34.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the appeal and did not reduce the sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction can be set aside due to an illegality in the investigation, such as non-compliance with Section 5A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, if the illegality has not caused any prejudice or miscarriage of justice to the accused.

facts: The accused-appellants were convicted under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
They appealed their conviction, arguing that the investigation was illegal because it did not comply with the procedural requirements of Section 5A of the Act.
law: The Court cited the established legal principle that an illegality committed during an investigation does not affect the competence and jurisdiction of the court to try the accused.

A conviction resulting from a trial that followed a procedurally flawed investigation will not be invalidated unless the illegality is shown to have caused a 'miscarriage of justice' or 'prejudice' to the accused.
application: The Court examined the record and found no material to suggest that the accused were prejudiced by the alleged non-compliance with Section 5A.
The Court determined that no miscarriage of justice had occurred in the case as a result of the procedural irregularity in the investigation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument and held that the conviction cannot be set aside. The Court reasoned that a procedural illegality in an investigation, such as non-compliance with Section 5A, is not a sufficient ground to overturn a conviction unless the accused can prove that this illegality resulted in actual prejudice or a miscarriage of justice, which they failed to do in this case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence imposed on the appellants should be reduced.

facts: The appellants made a formal request ('prayer') to the Supreme Court for their sentence to be reduced.
application: The Court considered the request but found no 'cogent ground,' meaning no convincing or strong reason, to interfere with the sentence that had been imposed by the lower courts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' request to reduce their sentence because they failed to provide a convincing reason for the Court to interfere with it.

cases.case_name: H. N. Rishbud and Inder Singh v. The State of Delhi
cases.principle: The invalidity of the preceding investigation would not vitiate the conviction of the accused as a result of the trial unless the illegality in the investigation has caused prejudice to the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An illegality committed during the course of an investigation does not affect the competence and jurisdiction of the court to try the accused. Therefore, where a trial has proceeded to termination, the invalidity of the preceding investigation will not vitiate the conviction unless the illegality in the investigation has caused prejudice to the accused or a miscarriage of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An illegality committed during the course of an investigation, such as non-compliance with Section 5A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, does not affect the competence and jurisdiction of the court to try the accused. Therefore, where a trial has proceeded to termination, the invalidity of the preceding investigation will not vitiate the conviction unless the illegality can be shown to have caused prejudice or a miscarriage of justice to the accused.
legal_tests_applied: The invalidity of the preceding investigation would not vitiate the conviction of the accused as a result of the trial unless the illegality in the investigation has caused prejudice to the accused.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to demonstrate that they were prejudiced by the alleged non-compliance with the provisions of Section 5A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, as there was no material on the record to show any such prejudice or miscarriage of justice.
Regarding the sentence, the appellants failed to provide any cogent ground for the court to interfere with the sentence imposed by the lower courts.
why_respondent_won: The conviction was upheld because it is well-established that once a court has taken cognizance of a case and the trial has concluded, the result cannot be set aside due to an illegality in the investigation unless it caused a miscarriage of justice. Since no such miscarriage of justice occurred, the conviction could not be set aside on that score.
The sentence was upheld because the court saw no compelling reason to reduce it.
policy_considerations: An illegality committed in the course of investigation does not affect the competence and jurisdiction of the court to try the accused. This principle ensures that convictions resulting from a fair trial are not overturned on the basis of procedural errors in the investigation that did not prejudice the accused.
